text: Lipschitz stability for identification of piecewise constant diffusion coefficient in parabolic equation from finitely many interior point measurements For a Lipschitz domain with given parameters, if the L2 norm difference of two weak solutions on a boundary part is bounded by epsilon, then the L-infinity norm difference of the corresponding coefficients on a specific inner boundary region is bounded by a function of epsilon. This function is the composition of eta with itself applied to epsilon. The result establishes a stability estimate for the coefficients based on the solutions' proximity. For sufficiently many boundary conditions and an open set of boundary data, the measurement operator uniquely determines the coefficients of the elliptic equation. Stability estimates bound the differences in coefficients by the differences in measurements. This holds when the coefficients are near certain reference classes, such as constant diffusion, scalar isotropic diffusion, or specific smoothness classes. The number of required boundary conditions depends on the spatial dimension. For a Lipschitz domain D, given functions a and b in class A1, and a positive bounded function f, the L2 norm of the difference between a and b is bounded by a constant times the H01 norm of the difference between their corresponding solutions raised to the power one-sixth. The constant depends on the domain, dimension, ellipticity parameters, and the lower bound of f. The inequality also involves a constant C0 from a prior definition. This result provides a stability estimate for the inverse problem of recovering coefficients from solutions. The fundamental solution of a divergence-form parabolic equation with a measurable, uniformly elliptic coefficient matrix satisfies a specific derivative estimate. The coefficient matrix is assumed to be Lipschitz continuous in the spatial variable. The constants in the estimate depend only on the ellipticity constant, the dimension, and the Lipschitz constant.

text: Lipschitz stability for the inverse problem of identifying a piecewise constant conductivity coefficient in a parabolic equation from interior or boundary point measurements The inverse Robin problem for parabolic equations is locally Lipschitz stable. This holds for all coefficients in a neighborhood of a given coefficient. The stability constant depends on the lower bound and the neighborhood size. For a Lipschitz domain D, given functions a and b in class A1, and a positive bounded function f, the L2 norm of the difference between a and b is bounded by a constant times the H01 norm of the difference between their corresponding solutions raised to the power one-sixth. title: Per-sample bounded LM in log-conductivity with box-prior posterior mean reaches near the Cramér–Rao floor
text: Inverting the forward map F(k) one sample at a time gets close to the information limit. The method is bounded Levenberg–Marquardt in log k with multistart, followed by importance-sampled posterior mean under the uniform box prior. We hypothesise val rel_l2 <= 0.035, within a factor of about 1.9 of the CRB floor of 0.0185, and well inside the 0.05 success threshold. The posterior-mean estimator should beat the MLE mode on k1 and k4. Those parameters are the least determined and the most often near the bounds, so truncating their posterior to the box shrinks their error. The forward model is known exactly and is available. It has 4 unknowns, i.i.d. Gaussian noise with sigma=0.001, and an explicit FD solver on 40×200 (cheap). The Fisher condition number is about 62, which is mild, and the CRB per-parameter relative std is 0.5–2%. The local likelihood is therefore well conditioned, and a Gauss-Newton/LM solver should be near-efficient once it is in the basin. Using log k enforces positivity. It also makes the multiplicative scale of k (range 0.5 to 2, a 4× ratio) closer to uniform in sensitivity. Sensor geometry explains why k1 and k4 are weak. The sensors sit at grid indices 5, 15, 25, 35, one per 10-cell segment at its centre. The pulse starts at x=0.5, so the outer segments see small amplitudes and gradients that are damped by the Dirichlet ends. Near the box edges the Gaussian Laplace posterior is truncated, which favours the MMSE estimator over the mode under the stated i.i.d. uniform prior. context.forward matches the simulator that generated the data (same grid, time steps and sensor times); i.e. there is no model error. Noise is exactly i.i.d. Gaussian with sigma = 0.001, so least squares is the MLE. The misfit is locally convex in log k within the prior box for most samples, and multistart=3 catches the rest. Per-sample LM over 750 val and 750 test samples fits in the 400 worker-second budget across 6 workers.

title: An amortised learned inverse plus a few LM steps matches per-sample physics accuracy and removes local-minimum failures
text: A torch MLP on log-temperature features learns a smooth approximation of the inverse map F^{-1}. It will not reach the CRB on its own; we expect val rel_l2 around 0.04–0.08, limited by finite training data and the weak k1/k4 signal. Starting from it, 10 LM iterations in log k will converge to the global basin for almost all samples. We predict the hybrid improves rel_l2 by at least 40% relative to the best pure data-driven model, and reaches <= 0.035 with fewer forward evaluations than cold-start multistart. In 4 dimensions with mild conditioning, the inverse map is smooth over the box, so a neural regressor gives an initial guess with about 5% error. That lies inside the Newton-Kantorovich basin of the least-squares misfit. With a good initial guess, a couple of Gauss-Newton steps are enough to reach the efficient estimator. Each step cuts the error quadratically down to the noise floor, so the learned model's bias is removed by the physics. Log features compress the dynamic range of the sensor signals: amplitudes decay with time and are small at the outer sensors. Combined with log k targets, they make the map closer to linear in the dominant scaling direction (k·t time-rescaling). 3000 training simulations are enough for the MLP to land in the LM basin of attraction for more than 98% of samples. Log features are well defined: the sensor readings stay positive with high probability, given small noise and a positive Gaussian IC. Otherwise the harness clips them. LM refinement using context.forward is consistent with the data-generating simulator. Noise augmentation at the true sigma helps the MLP generalise to noisy inputs.
